tasks.pr_text:
fix(bigquery): parse date parts by argument position
### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #5015.

Builds on the discussion in the closed, unmerged #8219 and #8654, including the authors' and reviewers' feedback on argument positions and `SAFE.` dispatch.

BigQuery currently recognizes date-part words in every function argument. As a result, CP01 can change a column such as `year` in `REGEXP_EXTRACT(year, ...)`, and CP02 cannot consistently recognize those arguments as identifiers.

This change restricts date-part recognition to the documented argument positions of the date/time difference, truncation, and `LAST_DAY` functions. Other arguments, including timestamp time-zone expressions, use the expression grammar. `SAFE.`-prefixed built-ins use the same positional grammar, while dataset-qualified UDFs keep ordinary expression arguments.

Existing unqualified chained calls use the corresponding grammar after omitting the first expression supplied by the chain. This preserves actual date units in calls such as `(year).DATE_DIFF(month, YEAR)` and `(year).LAST_DAY(WEEK(MONDAY))`. The existing `EXTRACT` and `INTERVAL` paths continue to recognize their date units.

Regression tests cover ordinary arguments, every affected function group, `SAFE.`, date-part positions, optional time zones, `WEEK(MONDAY)`, and existing chained calls. Both CP01 and CP02 expectations distinguish actual date units from column references.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

The change is limited to the BigQuery dialect grammar and its tests. Two existing generated parser fixtures now correctly classify ordinary arguments as column references: `parse_date(..., year)` in `parameters.yml`, and `DAY` passed to the existing generic `SAFE.DATEADD(...)` example in `select_safe_function.yml`. This does not add `DATEADD` as a BigQuery built-in.

The existing supported scope of unqualified chained calls is retained. Support for parenthesized multi-part c

issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

When run on a SQL file containing a line like REGEXP_EXTRACT(year, r"[0-9]{4}"), SQLFluff issued the CP01 linting error instead of the RF04 linting error.

### Expected Behaviour

When run on a SQL file containing a line like REGEXP_EXTRACT(year, r"[0-9]{4}"), SQLFluff should understand that year is not a parameter but a variable name and not issue the CP01 error.  RF04 would be issued.

### Observed Behaviour

I was linting BigQuery SQL with the line REGEXP_EXTRACT(year, r"[0-9]{4}") and unexpectedly got the CP01 error.  I believe this to be an error since year is the _variable name_ in this context, not a keyword.

### How to reproduce

Run the following to reproduce on online.sqlfluff.com:
- Set the dialect to BigQuery
- Run the following SQL:
```
SELECT REGEXP_EXTRACT(year, r"[0-9]{4}")
FROM
    table
```

### Dialect

BigQuery

### Version

sqlfluff, version 2.0.0 (but I think it's still broken in the newest version, see the online.sqlfluff.com example above)

### Configuration

```
[sqlfluff]
dialect = bigquery
templater = dbt
exclude_rules = LT01,LT02,AL01,CP02,LT05,RF04,AL07,ST06

[sqlfluff:layout:type:comma]
line_position = leading

[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.keywords]
capitalisation_policy = upper

[sqlfluff:rules:capitalisation.functions]
capitalisation_policy = upper
```

tasks.pr_text:
MySQL/MariaDB: parse the SOURCE client command
### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #8564

`SOURCE file_name` and the short form `\. file_name` are mysql/mariadb client commands that run another script. Right now they're unparsable, so any file that pulls in other files this way can't be linted.

- `SOURCE` is recognised between statements at the top level of a file, which is where the mysql client recognises it too. The keyword stays unreserved, so `CREATE TABLE source (source INT)` and `SELECT source FROM source` still parse.
- The file name isn't quoted and runs to the end of the line (or a `;`). It's matched with gaps disallowed, so it can contain spaces but stops at the newline.
- The mysql `FileSegment` makes the delimiter optional after `SOURCE` only. Every other statement still needs one, e.g. `SELECT 1\nSELECT 2;` is still unparsable, same as main.
- File name parts get their own type, plus `spacing_within = any` for `source_file_name` in the default config, so LT01/CP rules leave file names alone.
- `\.` needed a small lexer matcher, since a backslash doesn't lex otherwise.

I didn't lex the whole `SOURCE ...` line as one token. The lexer can't tell where a statement starts, so a column called `source` at the start of a line (`source = 'web'` in a WHERE) would have been swallowed. I followed the psql meta-commands in the postgres dialect and Oracle's `ExecuteFileSegment` instead.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

- New `[sqlfluff:layout:type:source_file_name]` section in the default config. (Couldn't call the type `*_path`, since config keys ending in `_path` get resolved as file paths.)
- Two things I hit in the Rust side and worked around rather than fixed:
  - Rust `OneOf` skips leading whitespace/newlines by default and Python's doesn't. Without `allow_gaps=False` the Rust parser carried the file name onto the next line. The Rust fixture parity test caught it.

issues.title: MySQL/MariaDB: support the `SOURCE` client command
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### Description

`SOURCE file.sql` is how a MySQL/MariaDB script includes another script. It is
the mechanism multi-file schemas and programs are assembled with, so it
appears in exactly the top-level files that drive everything else.

It's terminated by an end of line or a semicolon, so it can't easily be fixed
without lexer support.  It also allows spaces, and does not accept surrounding
quotes, as they are interpreted as part of the filename (not by sqlfluff, but by
MySQL/MariaDB).

SQLFluff currently reports the whole line as an unparsable section:

```
L:   1 | P:   1 |  PRS | Line 1, Position 1: Found unparsable section: 'SOURCE
                       | schema/tables.sql'
```

It is a client command rather than server SQL, but so is `DELIMITER`, which
SQLFluff already models as `DelimiterStatement`.

All of these are currently unparsable, on both `mysql` and `mariadb`:

```sql
SOURCE setup.sql
SOURCE schema/tables.sql;
source lowercase/path.sql
SOURCE path/with spaces/file.sql
\. schema/tables.sql
```

Paths may be relative or absolute, the trailing semicolon is optional, and an
unquoted path may contain spaces, because the client reads to end of line.

I think it needs to lex like this to fit MySQL/MariaDB, **at start of
statement** (case insensitive):
`(?i)[ \t]*(SOURCE|\\\.)[ ]+([^\n\r;]+?)[ ]*(\r\n|\n|;)`

It is genuinely statement-positional rather than line-positional — this runs
the SOURCE, so an anchor on the preceding newline would miss it:

```
> select 1; source 'abcd';
ERROR: Failed to open file ''abcd'', error: 2
```

Though actually turning that into code is nontrivial.  Note the lazy file capture
to avoid swallowing the later spaces.  Case-insensitivity will need an inline
`(?i)`: `RegexLexer` compiles with `regex.DOTALL` only and takes no flags
argument.

A SOURCE directive with multiple semicolons is parsed only up to the first
semicolon, the second one is read by the sql client as another statement.

Multiple spaces are allowed both before and after the keyword, but there
must be at least one after the keyword.

The argument is arbitrary text rather than SQL tokens, which is why this needs
the lexer.  `SOURCE schema/tables.sql` happens to lex because `/` and `.` have
matchers, but a filename need not be made of those — and then it fails exactly
the way `DELIMITER $$` does:

```
SOURCE a$b.sql       Unable to lex characters: '$b.sql'
SOURCE C:\db\x.sql    Unable to lex characters: '\db\x.sql'
```

`DELIMITER` is the model: `DelimiterStatement` is inserted into
`StatementSegment`, so it is only offered where a statement can begin. That is
what keeps it unambiguous even though `DELIMITER` is an unreserved keyword and
`SELECT delimiter FROM t` parses fine. A `SourceStatement` in the same place
gets the same protection, which matters because `SOURCE` is unreserved too.

The one wrinkle is the path's end. `DELIMITER` sidesteps it —
`match_grammar = Ref.keyword("DELIMITER")` never consumes its own argument —
but `SOURCE` has to capture the path, and the terminator is a newline whenever
the optional semicolon is omitted. There is precedent for matching newlines
from a grammar: postgres defines

```python
MultilineConcatenateNewline=TypedParser("newline", NewlineSegment, type="newline"),
MultilineConcatenateDelimiterGrammar=AnyNumberOf(
    Ref("MultilineConcatenateNewline"), min_times=1, allow_gaps=False
),
```

for multiline string concatenation, which is the same need.

#3599 is the same kind of problem and may want the same solution:
https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues/3599#issuecomment-5430153824

`\.` is the documented alias for `SOURCE` and means the same thing, so it is in
the syntax above. It needs one extra piece — the backslash currently fails with
`Unable to lex characters`, so it wants a fixed-string matcher. That is a
one-liner of a kind `dialect_mysql.py` already has six sets of
(`StringLexer("walrus_operator", ":=", ...)` and friends), it is stateless, and
`build_lexers.py` handles `StringLexer` so the Rust side comes along for free.
Nothing like the stateful matcher #3599 needs. Worth doing at the same time.

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

Sort of.  I'm trying to make MySQL/MariaDB first class in the functions/procedures
realm, but I know @Mynk11 is working on a very similar problem with DELIMITER,
and I think i should stay out of this while that's occurring.  It also looks easier to
subtly get wrong than my other PR's so I'd prefer that someone else do it.  That
being said, sure, maybe.

### Use case

Linting a multi-file schema where scripts include `SOURCE` lines. Those files are
currently unparsable in their entirety, so they have to be excluded, which means
the files that define the load order are the ones that get no checking at all.

### Dialect

mysql and mariadb

- [ ] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

fix(snowflake): indent scripting CASE WHEN/ELSE branches (LT02)
### Summary

In the Snowflake dialect, LT02 indentation for a scripting `CASE` statement is inverted: it expects (and `sqlfluff fix` enforces) the `WHEN`/`ELSE` branches at the **same** column as `CASE`, which is the opposite of correct and contradicts the dialect's own fixture.

Fixes #8690.

### Root cause

`ScriptingCaseStatementSegment` (`src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_snowflake.py`) placed `Indent`/`Dedent` only around each `THEN` body — there was **no `Indent` wrapping the branch list itself**. So `WHEN`, `ELSE`, and `END` stayed at the `CASE` column. Sibling constructs (`IF`, `WHILE`, `FOR`, the ANSI `CASE` expression) all wrap their branch block in an indent; this one was missing it.

### Fix

Two meta placements: `Indent` after the optional case value, and `Dedent` immediately before `END`. Now `WHEN`/`ELSE` sit one level below `CASE`, their bodies two levels, and `END [CASE]` returns to the `CASE` column — matching the fixture. No reflow/core changes.

### Verification

- Reporter's SQL: `lint` now clean (was 4 LT02 flags); `fix` is a no-op (was pulling `WHEN`/`ELSE` to `CASE`'s column).
- `test/fixtures/dialects/snowflake/scripting_control_flow.sql`: **22 LT02 violations → 0**.
- Added 3 cases to `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/LT02-indent.yml` (value form pass, searched form pass, fail→fix).
- `pytest test/rules/ -k LT02`: 259 passed. Snowflake dialect parse tests: 750 passed. `ruff` clean.

issues.title: Snowflake - CASE statement indent broken, doesn't even match fixture
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

LT02 wants the `WHEN`/`ELSE` branches of a Snowflake scripting `CASE` statement at the same level as `CASE`.  This is the opposite of what everything else does.

Below is what is generally correct, but rejected by LT02 on snowflake.
```sql
BEGIN
    CASE (v)
        WHEN 1 THEN
            x := 2;
        ELSE
            x := 3;
    END CASE;
END;
```

`sqlfluff lint --dialect snowflake --rules LT02` flags every line inside the `CASE`, and `fix` pulls `WHEN`/`ELSE` back to `CASE`'s column. Snowflake's own fixture is written the indented way, and LT02 flags its `CASE` statements too (`test/fixtures/dialects/snowflake/scripting_control_flow.sql`, around lines 72, 86 and 155).

issues.title: Rust parser diverges from Python parser on Databricks `INSERT ... REPLACE ON <condition> (subquery)`
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

Databricks supports `INSERT INTO ... REPLACE ON <boolean_expression>` where the source can be either a normal query or a parenthesized query with an optional source alias:

```text
REPLACE ON boolean_expression
{ (query) [source_alias] | query }
```

I originally worked on aligning the Databricks `INSERT` grammar with the documented syntax in #8264. During review, it was identified that the parenthesized query form after `REPLACE ON` did not parse correctly.

I am working on the follow-up fix in [timothyvries/sqlfluff#5](https://github.com/timothyvries/sqlfluff/pull/5).

The underlying problem is that `ExpressionSegment` used for the `REPLACE ON` condition can consume the opening parenthesis of the following query. For example:

```sql
INSERT INTO TABLE students AS t
REPLACE ON t.name = s.name
(SELECT * FROM people) AS s;
```

Without a boundary between the condition and the query, the parser can interpret the parenthesis as belonging to the preceding identifier, effectively treating it like:

```text
s.name(SELECT ...)
```

rather than treating `t.name = s.name` as the complete boolean expression followed by a separate parenthesized query.

My current fix bounds the expression using `ParseMode.GREEDY` and terminators (before i also tried with SelectableGrammar instead of individual terminators) for tokens that can start the following query:

```python
Sequence(
    Ref("ExpressionSegment"),
    parse_mode=ParseMode.GREEDY,
    terminators=[
        Ref.keyword("SELECT"),
        Ref.keyword("VALUES"),
        Ref.keyword("WITH"),
        Ref("StartBracketSegment"),
    ],
),
Ref("SelectableGrammar"),
```

This produces the intended parse with the Python parser and the Python dialect parse suite passes.

However, when the same fixture is run using the Rust parser, it produces a different parse result and the Rust-backed CI suite fails.

I am therefore looking for guidance on either restructuring this grammar so that both parser implementations behave consistently, or identifying why the Rust parser handles this boundary differently.

### Expected Behaviour

SQLFluff's Databricks dialect should support the documented `INSERT ... REPLACE ON` forms, including both an unparenthesized query:

```sql
INSERT INTO TABLE students AS t
REPLACE ON t.name = s.name
SELECT * FROM people AS s;
```

and a parenthesized query with an optional source alias:

```sql
INSERT INTO TABLE students AS t
REPLACE ON t.name = s.name
(SELECT * FROM people) AS s;
```

In the second example, the parse tree should treat:

```text
t.name = s.name
```

as the `REPLACE ON` boolean expression, and:

```text
(SELECT * FROM people) AS s
```

as the source query and its alias.

The Python and Rust parser implementations should produce equivalent parse trees for this syntax.

### Observed Behaviour

Without explicitly bounding the `REPLACE ON` expression, the opening parenthesis of the following query can be consumed as part of `ExpressionSegment`.

This causes the parser to interpret the query as though it were function arguments attached to the final identifier of the condition rather than as the separate source query.

I can prevent this on the Python side by making the condition a greedy sequence with query-start terminators. With the current implementation in  [timothyvries/sqlfluff#5](https://github.com/timothyvries/sqlfluff/pull/5):

- the Python parser parses the statement correctly;
- the Python dialect parse suite succeeds;
- the generated Python fixture represents the condition and parenthesized query separately;
- the Rust-backed parser suite does not produce the same result and fails in CI.

So the remaining blocker is parser parity between the Python and Rust implementations for this grammar.

### How to reproduce

The minimal SQL example is:

```sql
INSERT INTO TABLE students AS t
REPLACE ON t.name = s.name
(SELECT * FROM people) AS s;
```

This is also covered by the Databricks `insert_into.sql` fixture in  [timothyvries/sqlfluff#5](https://github.com/timothyvries/sqlfluff/pull/5).

On the `feature/bynamereplace` branch, the relevant grammar currently uses:

```python
Sequence(
    Ref("ExpressionSegment"),
    parse_mode=ParseMode.GREEDY,
    terminators=[
        Ref.keyword("SELECT"),
        Ref.keyword("VALUES"),
        Ref.keyword("WITH"),
        Ref("StartBracketSegment"),
    ],
),
Ref("SelectableGrammar"),
```

The standard Python dialect parse suite succeeds, while the equivalent Rust-backed dialect test fails in CI.

The relevant work is:

- Original Databricks `INSERT` implementation: #8264
- Current follow-up / reproduction:  [timothyvries/sqlfluff#5](https://github.com/timothyvries/sqlfluff/pull/5)
- Branch: feature/bynamereplace

### Dialect

databricks

### Version

SQLFluff 4.3.0

The current reproduction is against the source branch feature/bynamereplace in  [timothyvries/sqlfluff#5](https://github.com/timothyvries/sqlfluff/pull/5).

The failing CI run uses Python 3.14 for the dialect parse suite, with the Rust parser (sqlfluffrs 4.3.0).

### Configuration

No special configuration is required.

The issue is in the dialect/parser grammar and does not depend on templating or linting-rule configuration.

issues.title: LT01 removes the space between `VARIADIC` and `ARRAY`, corrupting variadic array literal arguments
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

`sqlfluff fix` with **LT01** (enabled by default) **corrupts** a variadic array literal argument in the `postgres` dialect by deleting the space between `VARIADIC` and `ARRAY`, fusing the two keywords into a single identifier:

```sql
-- in
SELECT f(VARIADIC ARRAY[1, 2]);
-- out
SELECT f(VARIADICARRAY[1, 2]);
```

`VARIADICARRAY` is no longer the same token: before the fix `VARIADIC` is a `keyword` and `ARRAY` is an `array_type`, afterwards the pair parses as one `naked_identifier`. The query changes meaning (and stops being a variadic call). The fix is reported as applied and `sqlfluff fix` exits 0.

The named-argument form is mangled too:

```
SELECT f(VARIADIC arr := ARRAY[1, 2]);  ->  SELECT f(VARIADICarr:=ARRAY[1, 2]);
```

### How to reproduce

```sh
$ printf 'SELECT f(VARIADIC ARRAY[1, 2]);\n' > v.sql
$ sqlfluff fix --dialect postgres --rules LT01 -f v.sql
== [v.sql] FIXED
$ cat v.sql
SELECT f(VARIADICARRAY[1, 2]);
```

Verified with LT01 alone (no other rules involved). Also reproduces with the default rule set. Affected dialects: **postgres**, **redshift** and **duckdb** (the three I checked where `VARIADIC` is a keyword). `ansi`, `snowflake` and `trino` don't fuse it, because `VARIADIC` isn't a keyword there.

Unaffected, for contrast: `SELECT f(ARRAY[1, 2]);`, `SELECT ARRAY[1, 2];` and `SELECT f(VARIADIC arr);` are all left alone.

### Cause

`TypedArrayLiteralSegment` in `src/sqlfluff/dialects/dialect_postgres.py:7424` extends the ansi segment by inserting the optional variadic prefix **inside** the segment:

```python
match_grammar = ansi.TypedArrayLiteralSegment.match_grammar.copy(
    insert=[
        Sequence(
            Ref.keyword("VARIADIC"),
            Sequence(Ref("NakedIdentifierSegment"), Ref("WalrusOperatorSegment"), optional=True),
            optional=True,
        )
    ],
    before=Ref("ArrayTypeSegment"),
)
```

The parse tree is therefore:

```
expression:
    typed_array_literal:
        keyword: 'VARIADIC'
        whitespace: ' '
        array_type:
            keyword: 'ARRAY'
            array_literal: ...
```

while `src/sqlfluff/core/default_config.cfg:228` sets

```
[sqlfluff:layout:type:typed_array_literal]
spacing_within = touch
```

`spacing_within` spans from the first to the last token of the segment, so "touch" now also applies at the `VARIADIC` / `ARRAY` boundary and LT01 deletes that space. The `array_literal` is a *sibling* of `array_type`, not a child, so `array_type`'s own `spacing_within` can't be relied on to keep `ARRAY[...]` tight instead.

### Two fixes I tried that don't work

1. **Dropping the `typed_array_literal` layout section.** Fixes the corruption but regresses the intended tightening from #5005: `SELECT ARRAY[1, 2];` becomes `SELECT ARRAY [1, 2];`.
2. **Wrapping the prefix in its own segment** (new `variadic_array_literal_prefix` type + `spacing_after = single`). The parent's `spacing_within` still wins at that boundary, so `VARIADIC ARRAY` is still fused, and the `:=` boundary then loses its space instead (`VARIADIC arr :=ARRAY[1, 2]`).

So the usable direction seems to be to keep `VARIADIC` **outside** the `typed_array_literal` segment — e.g. a `variadic_array_literal` (or prefix) segment referenced from the same places that reference `TypedArrayLiteralSegment`, so `typed_array_literal` again covers exactly `ARRAY` + `[...]` and its `spacing_within = touch` applies only there. That's a grammar change across the reference sites, so I'd rather not guess at it: happy to implement it if you point me at the preferred shape, or to try a narrower variant you prefer.

### Dialect

postgres (also redshift, duckdb).

### Configuration

None. LT01 is enabled by default.

### Version

```
sqlfluff, version 4.3.0
```
Measured on `main` at `2e2275713`.

### Are you willing to work on and submit a PR to address the issue?

- [X] Yes I am willing to submit a PR! (pending direction on the fix shape above — I'd rather not submit a speculative grammar change)

### AI assistance disclosure

Per CONTRIBUTING.md ("AI-Assisted Contributions"): this report was drafted with AI assistance. I validated it manually — reproduced the corruption through the CLI, confirmed the before/after segment types with the parser API, checked the three affected dialects plus three unaffected ones, and tried both candidate fixes above to confirm they don't work. I'm happy to provide the test cases I used for the dialect matrix.

tasks.pr_text:
LT02: keep unrendered Jinja block indentation stable
### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #5410.

LT02 can infer zero indentation for a conditional block whose SQL is entirely
skipped in a rendered variant. The resulting fix can move only its opening tag,
or move an SQL-empty enclosing block's tags, even though a fully rendered variant
accepts their existing source indentation. On subsequent calls, different
variants can alternately remove and restore that indentation.

Extend the existing skipped-source filtering to exclude a complete matched block
occurrence spanning only template lines when it contains skipped source and its
tags occupy different source lines. Boundaries must match by UUID and occurrence;
visible SQL, incomplete spans, same-line blocks and unrelated boundary content
remain outside this exclusion. Existing loop handling and source-patch merging
are unchanged.

Tests cover the original issue, nested and explicitly configured intermediate
renderings, repeated UUIDs, occurrence isolation, visible-body corrections,
if/else, LT02 with LT09, boundary content, and existing CRLF-to-LF normalization.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

An eligible SQL-empty occurrence abstains from changing that block's indentation;
a rendered alternative remains lintable. With only an unrendered variant, the
existing block indentation is preserved rather than guessed. This does not
change Jinja evaluation, parser grammar, general fix safety or patch-merger
semantics, and does not implement the separate constructor work discussed in#4183.

CV06: keep a one-line block comment on the code's line before a newline semicolon
### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #8642.

With `multiline_newline: true`, CV06 keeps an inline comment on the code's line when the semicolon is on the next line (`FROM foo -- c` then `;`). A block comment in the same place was flagged instead, and the fix moved it after the terminator (`FROM foo` / `; /* c */`). It isn't TSQL-specific: ANSI does the same.

The cause is `_handle_preceding_inline_comments`. It treats a same-line comment as part of the code's line, but excludes every `block_comment`. That exclusion is right for a block comment that spans lines: `test_fail_newline_preceding_block_comment_custom_multiline` pins moving one, and the lexer splits it into one `block_comment` piece per line (`'/* multiline'`, `'comment'`, `'*/'`). A block comment that opens and closes on the code's line is a single piece, and it now gets the inline comment's treatment. The check is that the piece starts with `/*`, ends with `*/`, and closes every `/*` it opens. The last part matters in PostgreSQL and T-SQL, where comments nest: the first line of `/* outer /* inner */` + newline + `still outer */` also ends in `*/` but is not whole.

- `test_pass_newline_single_line_block_comment`: the issue's shape passes.
- `test_fail_newline_single_line_block_comment`: with a blank line before the `;`, the fix keeps the comment on the code's line.

RF03: don't unqualify correlated references in APPLY / LATERAL subqueries
### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #8626.

With `single_table_references = unqualified`, RF03 treated a subquery in the FROM clause as a single table select, even when it referenced tables of the outer query. T-SQL `CROSS APPLY` / `OUTER APPLY` and `LATERAL` joins allow that. The fix then removed those qualifiers, so `a.patientid = s.patientid` became `patientid = patientid`, which is always true. AL05 and ST05 could then make the result worse (see the issue).

RF03 already counts the parent query's tables as visible for subqueries in the SELECT / WHERE clauses. This PR does the same for FROM clause subqueries, but only when one of their references uses an outer table. In valid SQL, only correlated subqueries (APPLY / LATERAL) do that. issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

With `single_table_references = unqualified`, `sqlfluff fix` (rule RF03) removes the table qualifier from a correlated reference inside a T-SQL `OUTER APPLY` / `CROSS APPLY` subquery. The reference points to a table in the outer query, but RF03 treats the subquery as a single-table select and unqualifies it. The fixed SQL still parses, but its meaning changes: `a.patientid = s.patientid` becomes `patientid = patientid`, which is always true (for non-null values).

Other rules then make it worse. After RF03, AL05 removes the now-unused alias `a`. ST05 (`forbid_subquery_in = both`) then moves the subquery, which no longer looks correlated, into a CTE. On its own, ST05 correctly leaves the correlated subquery alone.

### Expected Behaviour

RF03 must not unqualify references to tables outside the current select, such as the outer query of an `APPLY`. For the same pattern with `WHERE EXISTS (...)`, RF03 keeps `s.patientid` correctly. `APPLY` should behave the same.

### Observed Behaviour

Input:

```sql
select s.patientid
from dbo.spoed as s
outer apply (
    select top 1 1 as heeft_afspraak
    from dbo.afspraken as a
    where a.patientid = s.patientid
) as lg
```

After `sqlfluff fix --rules RF03`:

```sql
select s.patientid
from dbo.spoed as s
outer apply (
    select top 1 1 as heeft_afspraak
    from dbo.afspraken as a
    where patientid = patientid
) as lg
```

`sqlfluff lint --rules RF03` reports:

```
L:   6 | P:  11 | RF03 | Qualified reference 'a.patientid' found in single table select. [references.consistent]
L:   6 | P:  26 | RF03 | Qualified reference 's.patientid' found in single table select. [references.consistent]
```

After `sqlfluff fix --rules RF03,AL05,ST05` (with `forbid_subquery_in = both`):

```sql
with lg as (
    select top 1 1 as heeft_afspraak
    from dbo.afspraken
    where patientid = patientid
)
select s.patientid
from dbo.spoed as s
outer apply lg
```

`CROSS APPLY` gives the same result. With the default `single_table_references = consistent`, RF03 does not change the file.

### How to reproduce

`.sqlfluff`:

```ini
[sqlfluff]
dialect = tsql

[sqlfluff:rules]
single_table_references = unqualified
```

Save the input above as `repro.sql`, then run:

```
sqlfluff fix repro.sql --rules RF03
```

tsql

The `.sqlfluff` shown above. Add `[sqlfluff:rules:structure.subquery]` with `forbid_subquery_in = both` to reproduce the ST05 step.

BigQuery: parse WITH expressions
### Brief summary of the change made

fixes #8608

BigQuery has a `WITH` expression. It assigns one or more variables and returns its last argument, for example `WITH(a AS 1, b AS a + 1, a + b)`. The bigquery dialect has no grammar for it. Most of these statements are unparsable, and `WITH(a AS (SELECT 1), a)` parses as a call to a function named `WITH`.

This change adds `WithExpressionSegment`, with the type `with_expression`. The grammar is `WITH ( variable_name AS expression [, ...], result_expression )`, from the [BigQuery operators page](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/reference/standard-sql/operators#with_expression). ### Description

In BigQuery, the WITH keyword isn't just for CTEs, it can also be used as a way to create temporary variables when creating a column for example.

Keep the token text before a Jinja tag inside the token
### Brief summary of the change made

fixes #8611

A token can span a Jinja tag, as in `b{% if true %}c{% endif %}`. The lexer then yields the placeholder for the tag, and its indent or dedent, before the token. Their templated position is after the start of the token. `BaseSegment._position_segments` and `_iter_templated_patches` used that position as a boundary. A fix next to the token then deleted the text before the tag.

The change has three parts:

- A new helper, `inside_next_segment_flags` in `parser/helpers.py`, flags each zero-length segment that sits inside a later sibling. It makes one backward pass over the siblings.
- `_position_segments` and `_iter_templated_patches` skip such a segment, as they already skip the empty template placeholder from #6261. When the previous sibling is such a segment, a new segment starts at its end point.
- With the correct position, `_iter_templated_patches` dropped a gap in the templated file after an insertion, so a moved token kept its old text. The patch now covers that gap. LT02 plus LT09 on `select\nb{# note #}c` needs this part.

Measured with `Linter.lint_string(sql, fix=True)` and the `ansi` dialect:

| rules | input | `main` at `2e2275713` | this branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| LT02 | `select\nb{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select\n    {% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select\n    b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` |
| LT01 | `select a  , b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select a, {% if true %}c{% endif %}` | `select a, b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` |
| LT01 | `select b{% if true %}c{% endif %}, a  , x` | `select {% if true %}c{% endif %}, a, x` | `select b{% if true %}c{% endif %}, a, x` |
| LT05 | the trailing comment example from the issue | `-- trailing comment here` is deleted | the comment moves to its own line |

issues.title: `sqlfluff fix` deletes source text when a token spans a Jinja tag
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

`sqlfluff fix` deletes source text when a token spans a Jinja tag. A token spans a tag when the rendered SQL joins the text on both sides of the tag. For example, `b{% if true %}c{% endif %}` renders as the one identifier `bc`.

A fix deletes the part of such a token before the tag in two cases:

- The fix puts a new segment directly before the token. LT02 does this in q1.sql, and LT05 does it in q3.sql and q4.sql.
- The fix changes another segment in the same clause. In q2.sql, LT01 removes the spaces before the comma. The space before `b` does not change, but the `b` is deleted. `select b{% if true %}c{% endif %}, a  , x` loses its `b` too, with the fix after the token.

`sqlfluff fix` reports the violation as fixed and exits with 0. After the fix, `sqlfluff lint` with the same rule reports nothing.

I found this with LT05 and a skipped `{% if false %}` block. A skipped block is not necessary. LT01 and LT02 delete text in the same way with `{% if true %}`.

### Expected Behaviour

`sqlfluff fix` keeps all source text which is not whitespace. For q1.sql below, the expected output is:

```sql
select
    b{% if true %}c{% endif %}
```

For q2.sql it is `select a, b{% if true %}c{% endif %}`. If a fix cannot keep the text, `sqlfluff fix` does not apply it and reports the violation as unfixable.

### Observed Behaviour

Each command in "How to reproduce" prints `FIXED` for its files and exits with 0. The files are then:

q1.sql loses the `b`:

```sql
select
    {% if true %}c{% endif %}
```

q2.sql loses the `b`:

```sql
select a, {% if true %}c{% endif %}
```

q3.sql loses the comment `-- trailing comment here`:

```sql
select a, b, c
from tbl
{% if false %} xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx{% endif %}
```

q4.sql loses the 65 `a` characters:

```sql
{% if false %}
    select
{% endif %}select 1
```

`sqlfluff render` shows the column `bc` in q1.sql and q2.sql before the fix, and `c` after it. With the default rules, q1.sql, q3.sql and q4.sql lose the same text. q2.sql instead gets a second `{% if true %}` tag, and `sqlfluff render` then fails with `Failed to parse Jinja syntax`.

q3.sql is the `trailing_comment` test input in #8605. `main` without #8605 gives the same output, so the loss does not come from #8605.

**Cause.** The lexer yields the placeholder for a tag before the token which spans the tag. The code is `_iter_segments` in `src/sqlfluff/core/parser/lexer.py`. The placeholder and its indent or dedent meta then sit between the whitespace and the token. Their templated position is after the start of the token. Two functions use that position as the end of a source range, so the range covers the start of the token:

- `BaseSegment._position_segments` in `src/sqlfluff/core/parser/segments/base.py` positions a new segment up to the next sibling with a position. In q1.sql, the new indent from LT02 gets source slice `7:8`, which is the `b`. The new newline from LT05 gets source slice `23:49` in q3.sql and `20:86` in q4.sql.
- `_iter_templated_patches` in `src/sqlfluff/core/linter/patch.py` walks into each parent segment which has a change. It treats the gap before the placeholder as a deletion. In q2.sql, the parent is the `select_clause`. It yields a `mid_point` patch for source slice `12:13`, which is the `b`.

#7582 added a guard at both places for #6261. The guard skips only a `templated` placeholder which renders to an empty string. Here the placeholder is for a `block_start` or `block_end` tag. `generate_source_patches` then keeps the patch, because its source slice is inside one literal slice. In q3.sql and q4.sql, the token spans the tag only in the variant which renders the `{% if false %}` block.

The guard does not cover a Jinja comment either. With LT01, `select a  , b{# note #}c` loses its `b`. A `{% set x = 1 %}` tag gives a `templated` placeholder, and the guard keeps the `b`. The indent or dedent meta of the tag has the same templated position as its placeholder. With the guard widened to `block_start`, `block_end` and `comment` placeholders, q2.sql and q4.sql still lose their text.

### How to reproduce

```sh
cat > q1.sql <<'EOF'
select
b{% if true %}c{% endif %}
EOF
cat > q2.sql <<'EOF'
select a  , b{% if true %}c{% endif %}
EOF
cat > q3.sql <<'EOF'
select a, b, c from tbl  -- trailing comment here{% if false %} xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx{% endif %}
EOF
cat > q4.sql <<'EOF'
{% if false %}select aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa{% endif %}select 1
EOF
sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules LT02 q1.sql
sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules LT01 q2.sql
sqlfluff fix --dialect ansi --rules LT05 q3.sql q4.sql
```

### Dialect

ansi. postgres, bigquery, snowflake and tsql give the same output for q1.sql and q2.sql.

### Version

```
sqlfluff, version 4.3.0
Python 3.12.14
```

Measured on `main` at `2e2275713`. The `4.3.0` tag gives the same output for the four files.

### Configuration

None. There is no `.sqlfluff` file. The command line gives the dialect and the rule, and the templater is the default `jinja`.

issues.title: `pip install sqlfluff-templater-dbt` silently breaks a dbt-oss 2.x environment
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

Installing `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` into an environment that has **dbt-oss** silently breaks dbt. The templater requires `dbt-core>=1.4.1`, which dbt-oss does not satisfy, so pip installs dbt-core 1.x alongside it — and because both wheels own the same `site-packages/dbt/` path and overlap on 10 files, dbt-core's modules overwrite dbt-oss's. The install prints no warning, `pip check` passes, and `pip list` still reports `dbt-oss 2.0.4` as installed, but the `dbt` command is now dbt-core 1.12.5 and dbt-oss's engine is unreachable. Install order decides which one survives, so the reverse order breaks sqlfluff instead. I'm not asking for dbt-oss support here, only that the incompatibility fail loudly instead of quietly downgrading the user's dbt by a major version.

### Expected Behaviour

Installing `sqlfluff-templater-dbt` into an environment it cannot support should fail loudly — a pip resolution error, or a clear error when the templater loads.

### Observed Behaviour

In an environment with **dbt-oss**, the install succeeds, prints no warning, and leaves dbt broken. The user's `dbt` command silently becomes a different dbt at a different major version.

### How to reproduce

```
python -m venv env
./env/bin/pip install dbt-oss==2.0.4
./env/bin/dbt --version          # -> dbt-oss 2.0.4
./env/bin/pip install sqlfluff-templater-dbt==4.3.0
./env/bin/dbt --version          # -> Core: installed: 1.12.5
```
Nothing in the second install signals a problem. Afterwards:

- **No pip conflict warning**, and `pip check` reports "No broken requirements found".
- **`pip list` still shows `dbt-oss 2.0.4` as installed**, so anything that inspects the environment rather than running it — CI checks, lockfile audits, a human reading `pip list` — sees a healthy env.
- **The `dbt` CLI is now dbt-core 1.12.5.** dbt-oss's Rust engine (`dbt/_core.abi3.so`) is still on disk but unreachable: `import dbt.runner` fails with `ImportError: cannot import name 'Manifest' from 'dbt.artifacts.schemas.manifest'`, because dbt-core's modules now shadow it.
- `mashumaro` is downgraded 3.22 -> 3.17 as a side effect.

Install order decides the winner, so the reverse order breaks sqlfluff instead. A `pip install -r requirements.txt` containing both is a coin flip.

### Dialect

Databricks

### Version

- sqlfluff 4.3.0, sqlfluff-templater-dbt 4.3.0
- dbt-oss 2.0.4; dbt-core 1.12.5 (pulled in by the install)
- Python 3.12, macOS 15 (arm64), pip 26.2.1

n/a

issues.title: dbt templater fails with `DbtCatalogIntegrationNotFoundError` when using  `catalogs.yml`
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

(disclaimer: used AI for debugging and bug description, but everything has been reviewed and verified by me)

With the dbt templater, `sqlfluff lint` fails for the whole project if any model sets `catalog_name` to a catalog defined in `catalogs.yml`. The failure happens while dbt parses the project, before any file is linted. Excluding the file or using `.sqlfluffignore` doesn't help.

The dbt CLI (`dbt compile`, `dbt run`, `dbt build`) works fine on the same project.

**Root cause:** the dbt CLI loads `catalogs.yml` and registers each catalog with the adapter before parsing:

- It calls `load_catalogs_v2()` or `load_catalogs()`, then `adapter.bridge_v2_catalog()` and
  `adapter.add_catalog_integration()`.
- This happens in `dbt/cli/requires.py::setup_manifest` and `dbt/parser/manifest.py::parse_manifest`.

`DbtTemplater` does none of this. It calls `register_adapter()` in `dbt_config` and then
`ManifestLoader.get_full_manifest()` in `dbt_manifest`. The adapter therefore only knows its built-in catalogs
(`info_schema` and `managed_iceberg` for BigQuery). While parsing each node, dbt calls
`adapter.build_catalog_relation()`, which asks the adapter for the custom catalog and fails because it was never
registered.

This affects both the v1 `catalogs.yml` format and the v2 format (`flags.use_catalogs_v2: true`), because the
templater skips both loading paths.

### Expected Behaviour

`sqlfluff lint` compiles the project the same way `dbt compile` does, including catalogs from `catalogs.yml`, and lints the models normally.

### Observed Behaviour

Got error:
```text
=== [dbt templater] Sorting Nodes...
User Error: dbt failed during project compilation. Consider  running  `dbt debug` or `dbt compile` to get more information from dbt. dbt.adapters.catalogs._exceptions.DbtCatalogIntegrationNotFoundError: Runtime Error
  Catalog not found.Received: my_catalogExpected one of: info_schema, managed_iceberg?
```

### How to reproduce

1. Create a dbt project with these files.

   `dbt_project.yml`:

   ```yaml
   name: "example"
   version: "1.0.0"
   config-version: 2
   profile: "example"
   flags:
     use_catalogs_v2: true
   ```

   `catalogs.yml`:

   ```yaml
   catalogs:
     - name: my_catalog
       type: biglake_metastore
       table_format: iceberg
       config:
         bigquery:
           external_volume: 'gs://my-bucket'
           file_format: parquet
   ```

   `models/my_model.sql`:

   ```sql
   {{ config(
       materialized = 'table',
       catalog_name = 'my_catalog',
       storage_uri = 'gs://my-bucket/my_model',
   ) }}

   SELECT 1 AS id
   ```

2. Add a BigQuery profile named `example` to `~/.dbt/profiles.yml`.
3. Run `dbt compile`. It succeeds.
4. Run `sqlfluff lint models/my_model.sql`. It fails with the error above.

**Workaround:** a `sitecustomize.py` placed on `PYTHONPATH` that wraps `dbt.adapters.factory.register_adapter` and
registers the catalogs itself. With it, linting works:

```python
import contextlib

from dbt.adapters import factory
from dbt.adapters.catalogs import DbtCatalogIntegrationAlreadyExistsError
from dbt.config.catalogs import load_catalogs_v2
from dbt.config.runtime import RuntimeConfig

_original = factory.register_adapter


def _register_adapter_with_catalogs(config, mp_context, adapter_registered_log_level=None):
    _original(config, mp_context, adapter_registered_log_level)
    if not isinstance(config, RuntimeConfig):
        return
    adapter = factory.get_adapter(config)
    for catalog in load_catalogs_v2(config.project_root, config.project_name, config.cli_vars):
        with contextlib.suppress(DbtCatalogIntegrationAlreadyExistsError):
            adapter.add_catalog_integration(adapter.bridge_v2_catalog(catalog))


factory.register_adapter = _register_adapter_with_catalogs
```

**Suggested fix:** in `DbtTemplater.dbt_manifest`, before calling `ManifestLoader.get_full_manifest()`, mirror what
`setup_manifest` does:

- If `use_catalogs_v2` is set, load the catalogs with `load_catalogs_v2` and register each one via
  `bridge_v2_catalog` and `add_catalog_integration`.
- Otherwise, load them with `load_catalogs` and register each one's active write integration.

### Dialect

`bigquery`

### Version

- sqlfluff 4.3.0
- sqlfluff-templater-dbt 4.3.0
- dbt-core 1.12.4
- dbt-adapters 1.24.5
- dbt-bigquery 1.12.0
- Python 3.13

### Configuration

`.sqlfluff`:

```ini
[sqlfluff]
dialect = bigquery
templater = dbt
max_line_length = 120
max_parse_depth = 510

[sqlfluff:templater:dbt]
project_dir = data
```

The rest of our config (rule exclusions and layout/capitalisation settings) doesn't affect this; the failure occurs
before any rules run.

- [ ] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

fix(RF01): support case-insensitive table and alias references
### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #8594.

Rule `RF01` previously compared table references and aliases using raw/unescaped strings without dialect case-folding. In SQL dialects where unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive, referencing an alias or table using a different letter case (for example, `SELECT CI.id FROM source_table AS ci JOIN second_table AS b ON ci.id = b.id;`) resulted in a false-positive violation because `targets` contained the declared case while `possible_references` contained the reference case.

This change includes dialect-normalized identifiers (via `raw_normalized()`) in:
- `_alias_info_as_tuples` for aliased table expressions
- `_table_ref_as_tuple` for table references
- `_get_table_refs` for multipart and simple table references
- `standalone_aliases` candidate targets

This allows case-insensitive matching for unquoted identifiers while preserving exact case matching for quoted identifiers.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

None. Quoted identifiers remain case-sensitive because their segments do not undergo casefolding.

issues.title: RF01: false positive when an alias/table reference differs in letter case from its declaration
issues.body:
### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.

### What Happened

`RF01` (`references.from`) reports a false-positive "reference not found" when
a table alias or table name is referenced using a different letter case than
it was declared with, even though the two spellings denote the same
identifier under the dialect's own identifier-casing rules.

```sql
SELECT CI.id
FROM source_table AS ci
JOIN second_table AS b ON ci.id = b.id;
```

On `dialect = ansi` this raises:

```
Reference 'CI.id' refers to table/view not found in the FROM clause or found
in ancestor statement.
```

even though `ci`/`CI` are the same identifier under ansi's own upper-folding
rule for unquoted identifiers, and the query is valid, executable SQL. The
same false positive reproduces for an unaliased table reference (e.g.
`SELECT SOURCE_TABLE.id FROM source_table ...`), and for other dialects
regardless of which way they fold (verified upper-folding `ansi`/`trino`/
`tsql` and lower-folding `postgres`).

### Expected Behaviour

An unquoted alias/table reference should resolve case-insensitively,
consistent with the dialect's own identifier-casefold rules -- the same way
sibling rules `RF02`/`RF07`/`ST07` already compare identifiers (via
`raw_normalized()`), and the same way real databases treat unquoted
identifiers as case-insensitive. A **quoted** identifier should keep matching
case-sensitively, since most dialects do not casefold those.

### Observed Behaviour

`RF01` flags the reference as undefined instead of resolving it, in every
case where the reference's case differs from the alias/table's declared
case. Reversing which side is upper/lower-case still fails, confirming this
isn't about one direction (declared-vs-used) but that identifier comparisons
inside `RF01` never case-fold at all.

### How to reproduce

```
$ sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi -
SELECT CI.id
FROM source_table AS ci
JOIN second_table AS b ON ci.id = b.id;
^D
```

Also reproduces with the alias/reference case direction reversed, with an
unaliased table (`SELECT SOURCE_TABLE.id FROM source_table;`), and on
`postgres`/`trino`/`tsql`.

### Dialect

`ansi` (reproduces on every dialect `RF01` runs against by default; verified
`ansi`, `postgres`, `trino`, `tsql`).

### Version

`sqlfluff`, version 4.3.0 (current `main`, commit `e2d032239`). Python 3.12.3.

### Configuration

Default configuration, `RF01` enabled (its default state).

### Impact and validation

Impact: contract-violation — `RF01`'s job is to distinguish valid FROM-clause
references from undefined ones, and it gets this wrong for identifiers the
dialect itself treats as equivalent.

Entry point / who reaches it: any user running `sqlfluff lint`/`fix` with
`RF01` enabled (its default state) on SQL where an unquoted alias or table
name is referenced with different letter case than it was declared with.
This is triggered via the plain CLI/API lint path, no special configuration
needed.

Negative control: reverting the fix and re-running
`pytest test/rules/yaml_test_cases_test.py -k RF01 -q` gives `3 failed, 116
passed`; with the fix restored, `119 passed`.

This issue was drafted with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude Code).
AI-assisted: locating the root cause and drafting this report. Manually
validated: I reproduced the false positive myself by directly running
`sqlfluff lint` against the queries above on four dialects with opposite
identifier-folding directions, and I manually validated which identifier
types each dialect casefolds by reading the dialect definitions myself.

I will open a PR fixing this shortly.

tasks.pr_text:
Postgres: reject col_name_keywords (e.g. BETWEEN) as bare data types (#6430)
## Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #6430.

Per the [PostgreSQL keyword appendix](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-keywords-appendix.html), `col_name_keyword`s (the "cannot be function or type name" class, e.g. `BETWEEN`, `COALESCE`, `NULLIF`) may not be used as bare type names. SQLFluff accepted them, so this parsed with no error:

```sql
CREATE TABLE test_table (
    type between NOT NULL
);
```

The ANSI `DatatypeIdentifierSegment` only excludes `NOT` from its identifier regex, so any other keyword fell through as a "user-defined type".

## Change

Override `DatatypeIdentifierSegment` for Postgres to additionally exclude the `non-reserved-(cannot-be-function-or-type)` keyword class.

Two deliberate scoping decisions:
- **Built-in types are unaffected** — `INT`, `VARCHAR`, `TIMESTAMP`, etc. are matched by explicit branches in `DatatypeSegment` *before* this identifier fallback is reached.
- **Reserved keywords are intentionally NOT excluded.** The `substring(... SIMILAR ... ESCAPE ...)` special form relies on matching reserved words as data-type identifiers, so excluding them would break it (verified against the existing `substring.sql` fixture).

## Dialect

PostgreSQL.

## Tests

Added `test_valid_column_types_parse` (built-in + user-defined types still parse) and `test_col_name_keyword_not_valid_datatype` (`between` as a type is now unparsable) to `test/dialects/postgres_test.py`.

The full Postgres suite passes locally (`pytest test/dialects/dialects_test.py -k postgres test/dialects/postgres_test.py` → 538 passed), and `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` are clean on the changed files.

issues.body:
## Bug

`RF03` (`references.consistent`) silently skips consistency checking for a
Jinja-templated, unqualified column reference, even though the rendered
identifier is a completely ordinary column name a user wrote themselves.

## Repro

```
$ cat jinja_case.sql
{% set my_col = 'customer_id' %}
SELECT {{ my_col }}, orders.total FROM orders

$ sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --templater jinja --rules RF03 jinja_case.sql
All Finished!

$ cat plain_case.sql
SELECT customer_id, orders.total FROM orders

$ sqlfluff lint --dialect ansi --rules RF03 plain_case.sql
L:   1 | P:   8 | RF03 | Unqualified reference 'customer_id' found in single
                       | table select. [references.consistent]
L:   1 | P:  21 | RF03 | Qualified reference 'orders.total' found in single table
                       | select which is inconsistent with previous references.
                       | [references.consistent]
```

Both files describe the exact same query (`customer_id` unqualified,
`orders.total` qualified, single table). The byte-identical query flags two
`RF03` violations when written plainly, and zero when the same identifier is
rendered through Jinja. Reproduces on current `main`.

## Why this happens

`_check_references()` in `src/sqlfluff/rules/references/RF03.py` skips any
unqualified reference where `ref.is_templated` is `True`:

```python
if this_ref_type == "unqualified" and ref.is_templated:
    continue
```

That guard was added in #7615 to stop the `placeholder` templater's
colon-style bind parameters (e.g. `:colname`, rendered as a bare identifier
that is not a real column) from being wrongly qualified/flagged — the PR
body, review thread and added tests are all scoped explicitly to the
`placeholder` templater. `ref.is_templated` is a generic marker shared by
every templater, though, so the same guard also silently exempts Jinja/dbt
`{{ var }}`-rendered column names — genuine identifiers the user intends to
select — from ever being checked. Nothing in #7615's discussion considers
Jinja; this is scope drift in an unconditional check, not a decision anyone
made about the Jinja/dbt case.

## Expected

The Jinja-rendered case should report the same two violations as the
non-templated equivalent. The `placeholder`-templater exemption #7615 added
should stay scoped to that templater.

I have a fix + regression fixture ready and will open a PR shortly.

fix(oracle): parse bare `/` in CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT as division
### Brief summary of the change made

Fixes #8373.

`Support Oracle slash batch delimiter after views` (#7945) added
`terminators=[Ref("BatchDelimiterGrammar")]` to the `SELECT` body of a
`CREATE VIEW` so that a trailing SQL*Plus `/` on its own line would stop the
`SELECT` and let the outer batch consume the slash as a delimiter.

That terminator is `Ref("SlashBufferExecutorSegment")`, which is just
`Ref("SlashSegment")`, so it also matches any bare `/` inside the `SELECT` —
including the arithmetic division operator. The `SELECT` closes early on
`1 / 100`, and everything after the first operand collapses into an
unparsable section. This is a regression against 4.2.0 and affects every
unparenthesised `/` in a `CREATE VIEW` body, including common Oracle patterns
like `sysdate - 1/24` and `nvl(bytes, 0) / 1024 / 1024`.

```
$ printf 'CREATE VIEW myview AS\nselect 1 / 100 as z from dual;\n' | sqlfluff parse --dialect oracle -
...
L:   2 | P:  12 |  PRS | Line 2, Position 12: Found unparsable section: '100 as z from
                       | dual;'
```

SQL*Plus documents the slash-buffer-executor as a command that must appear on
its own line, whereas the division operator only appears inside an expression.

at the start of the input. Division operators are never preceded by a newline
in a well-formed `SELECT` expression, so they no longer terminate the `SELECT`;
the slash-batch-delimiter fixture is unchanged because its `/` still stands
alone on its own line.

### Search before asking

- [x] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues) and found no similar issues.


### What Happened

While upgrading from 4.2.0 to 4.3.0, we found what looked like an [ST03](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff/issues/8250) false positive, but tracing it back, the real defect is in the parser: a bare (unparenthesized) `/` division operator in the SELECT/WHERE of a CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT ... statement (Oracle dialect) gets misparsed as the SQL*Plus slash-buffer-executor. Everything after it collapses into one opaque unparsable section, so any rule needing structure past that point, ST03 in our case; misbehaves as a downstream symptom. This is not every use of `/`: wrapping it in parens, or having it already sit inside a function call's parens, avoids it. Measured against our ~2,900 SQL files: 64 of 685 CREATE VIEW files containing a `/` are actually affected.

Examples:
`where sample_time > sysdate - 1/24` → **breaks** (bare, unparenthesized division)
`where sample_time > sysdate - (1/24)` → **parses fine** (wrapped in parens)
`round(write.value / 1024 / 1024) as write_mb` → **parses fine** (the whole division sits inside round(...)'s own parens)
`nvl(bytes, 0) / 1024 / 1024 as size_mb` → **breaks** (the nvl(...) call only wraps its own arguments, the / 1024 / 1024 trailing it is still bare/unparenthesized at the top level)


### Expected Behaviour

`/` inside `CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT` ... should parse as division, same as `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` and same as it did in 4.2.0.

### Observed Behaviour

A bare `/` is consumed as `slash_buffer_executor`; the same division wrapped in parens parses fine.

### How to reproduce

Three conditions required, removing any one fixes it:

1) Statement is CREATE VIEW ... AS SELECT ... (CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT is fine).
2) SELECT/WHERE contains /.
3) That / is not already inside parens (its own or a function call's).

repro.sql as 
```
CREATE VIEW myview AS
select 1 / 100 as z from dual;
```

`sqlfluff parse --dialect oracle repro.sql`
Result: PRS | Found unparsable section: '100 as z from dual;'. Expected: clean parse.

Isolation notes: `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` unaffected; `+`/`-`/`*` unaffected; bare `WITH ... SELECT (no CREATE VIEW`) unaffected; literal vs. column operand doesn't matter.

oracle

Introduced in 4.3.0. Confirmed clean in 4.2.0

fix(teradata): accept arbitrary single-line BTEQ dot-commands
### Brief summary of the change made

BTEQ has a large set of dot-prefixed control commands (`.LOGON`, `.SET`,
`.EXPORT`, `.IMPORT`, `.OS`, `.REMARK`, `.SHOW`, ...), each confined to a single
line. `BteqStatementSegment` previously only recognised a small enumerated
keyword set with narrowly-modelled arguments, so most real BTEQ commands
produced an unparsable section:

```
echo ".LOGON tdpid/user,pass" | sqlfluff parse --dialect teradata -
# ... unparsable
echo ".SET WIDTH 254"         | sqlfluff parse --dialect teradata -
# ... unparsable
```

This generalises `BteqStatementSegment` to:

- accept **any** command word after the leading dot (known control-flow
  keywords still keep their structured parse), and
- consume the remainder of the line as opaque arguments, terminating on the
  newline (or a semicolon) so it never absorbs the following statement.

The existing structured parses for `.RUN FILE=` (#8023) and
`.IF ... THEN .QUIT` are preserved unchanged.

fixes #1673

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

- A newline `TypedParser` grammar (`BteqNewlineGrammar`) is added so the opaque
  argument matcher stops at the end of the line rather than crossing into the
  next statement.
- As before this change, a BTEQ command still parses as a `bteq_statement`, so
  layout rules can flag spacing inside a command's arguments (e.g. `FILE=` in
  `.RUN FILE=POSTING`). This is unchanged pre-existing behaviour, not new.
- Newline-separated dot-commands are now supported. BTEQ dot-commands are
  terminated by the end of their line, so the Teradata `FileSegment` makes a
  statement's terminator optional (the same optional-delimiter approach the
  T-SQL dialect already uses). An authentic BTEQ script — newline-terminated
  dot-commands interleaved with semicolon-terminated SQL — now parses cleanly

tasks.pr_text:
fix(postgres): don't flag 'provider' as a keyword violation (RF04)
### Brief summary of the change made

Stops RF04 (references.keywords) from incorrectly flagging `provider` as a keyword when used as an identifier in PostgreSQL.

Fixes #7691

### What changed

1. Moved `PROVIDER` from `non-reserved` to `not-keyword` in the PostgreSQL keyword list. `PROVIDER` is not listed as a keyword in the official PostgreSQL documentation — it was added to sqlfluff's keyword list solely to make the `CREATE COLLATION ... PROVIDER = ...` grammar work.

2. Manually registered `ProviderKeywordSegment` in the postgres dialect using `StringParser("provider", KeywordSegment)`. This ensures the parser still recognizes `PROVIDER` as a keyword in the `CREATE COLLATION` context, while removing it from the `unreserved_keywords` set that RF04 checks against.

3. Added a test case to `RF04.yml` confirming that `provider` as a column name does not trigger RF04 in the postgres dialect.

### Are there any other side effects of this change that we should be aware of?

No. The parse tree is unchanged — `PROVIDER` is still parsed as a keyword in `CREATE COLLATION` statements and as an `naked_identifier` elsewhere. All 164 postgres dialect fixtures were regenerated and remain unchanged.

- [x] Included test cases: RF04 rule test case in `test/fixtures/rules/std_rule_cases/RF04.yml`
